etymology: Hebrew Yahweh-Mekaddishkem (יְהוָה מְקַדִּשְׁכֶם) — "The LORD Who Sanctifies You" (Exod 31:13; Lev 20:8).
biblical_def: The covenant name God speaks of Himself in Mosaic law: "I am the LORD that doth sanctify you." The setting-apart of Israel is His own active work, not their achievement. Anticipates Hebrews' insistence that Christ "sanctifieth" His people (Heb 10:14).
webster_summary: The LORD Who Sanctifies — God's active setting-apart of His people.
webster_full: The compound covenant name God speaks of Himself repeatedly in Mosaic law (Exod 31:13; Lev 20:8; 21:8): "I am the LORD that doth sanctify you." Israel's set-apartness is YHWH's own active work, not their achievement. Anticipates the new covenant's clearer revelation that Christ sanctifies His people through His own offering.
scriptures: Exodus 31:13

Speak thou also unto the children of Israel, saying, Verily my sabbaths ye shall keep: for it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations; that ye may know that I am the LORD that doth sanctify you.
Leviticus 20:8
And ye shall keep my statutes, and do them: I am the LORD which sanctify you.
1 Thessalonians 5:23-24
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly... Faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it.
corruption_summary: Sanctification frequently mis-attributed to the saint as primary actor; YHWH-Mekaddishkem names the actual primary Sanctifier.
corruption_paragraphs: Sermons regularly load sanctification onto the saint as primary work. The covenant name names the actual order: YHWH is Mekaddishkem — the Sanctifier — of you. The saint's part is response, cooperation, yielding; the primary verb is His.
Recover the order: He sanctifies; we are sanctified. The verb of the new covenant matches the verb of the old: "the very God of peace sanctify you wholly."
usage: He is the One who sanctifies; we are sanctified.
Sanctification is His verb first.
Read Lev 20:8 alongside 1 Thess 5:23.

etymology: Hebrew Yahweh-Tsabaoth (יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת) — "LORD of Hosts"; tsaba means army or host. Used 285+ times in the OT.
biblical_def: The most-frequent compound divine name — "the LORD of hosts" or "LORD of armies." The hosts are angelic armies, celestial bodies, and the assembled people. YHWH commands the armies of heaven; nothing is outside His command. "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge" (Ps 46:7).
webster_summary: The LORD of Hosts — commander of heaven's armies.
webster_full: The most-frequent compound divine name in the Hebrew Bible — appearing 285+ times. Tsaba means army or host: angelic armies, celestial bodies ("all the host of them"), and the assembled people of God. "The LORD of hosts" names YHWH as commander of every army that exists, visible and invisible. Particular favorite of the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi).
scriptures: Psalm 46:7
The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge.
1 Samuel 17:45
Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts.
Isaiah 6:3
Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
corruption_summary: Translations soften to "LORD Almighty" or "LORD of armies" without the cosmic-command force; the militant connotation gets domesticated.
corruption_paragraphs: "LORD of hosts" sounds antique; translators often render it "LORD Almighty." The Hebrew is sharper: YHWH commands armies. David walked toward Goliath in His name. Elisha's servant saw the host of YHWH on the mountain (2 Kings 6:17). The cosmic-command image is intentional.
Recover the military edge: when Scripture invokes YHWH-Tsabaoth, it is naming the commander of every army that exists. No force out-numbers Him; no power out-ranks Him.
usage: YHWH-Tsabaoth commands heaven's armies.
David's name-of-power against Goliath.
The seraphim cry it in Isaiah 6.

etymology: Hebrew El Elohe Yisrael (אֵל אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל) — "God, the God of Israel." Named by Jacob at the altar in Shechem (Gen 33:20).
biblical_def: The covenant name Jacob pronounced at the altar in Shechem after returning to the Promised Land — "God, the God of Israel." Jacob (renamed Israel) declares the same God of his fathers is his own God. A name of personal covenantal claim.
webster_summary: God, the God of Israel — Jacob's altar at Shechem.
webster_full: The compound covenant name Jacob pronounced at the altar he built in Shechem after his return to Canaan (Gen 33:20). The doubling — El, Elohe Yisrael — emphasizes that the same God who is God absolute is also the God of Israel personally. Jacob, renamed Israel, claims his fathers' God as his own.
scriptures: Genesis 33:20
And he erected there an altar, and called it El-elohe-Israel.
Genesis 28:21
So that I come again to my father's house in peace; then shall the LORD be my God.
Galatians 4:6
And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.
corruption_summary: Genealogical religion ("my parents' God") often substitutes for personal claim; El Elohe Israel insists on personal appropriation.
corruption_paragraphs: Inheriting religion is not the same as claiming God. Jacob's altar names the moment when his fathers' God became his own God. Each generation must make the same declaration; cultural Christianity is not yet Christianity.
Recover the personal claim: the LORD must be your God, not just your parents'. El Elohe Israel was Jacob's pronouncement; what is yours?
usage: El Elohe Israel — Jacob's personal claim.
Inherited religion is not yet personal faith.
Each generation must claim the God of the fathers.

etymology: Hebrew Azazel (עֲזָאזֵל) — "the goat that goes away" or possibly a proper name; the term Tyndale rendered "scape-goat" in Lev 16.
biblical_def: The second goat of the Day of Atonement ritual (Lev 16). After confession of Israel's sins over its head, it was driven into the wilderness, carrying the iniquities away. Distinct from the first goat sacrificed for sin. Tyndale coined the English "scape-goat" to render azazel.
webster_summary: The wilderness-goat of Yom Kippur; carries sin away.
webster_full: The second goat of the Day of Atonement ritual described in Leviticus 16. After Aaron confessed all the iniquities of Israel over its head, the goat was driven into the wilderness by a fit man — carrying the sins away to a land not inhabited. Distinct from the first goat sacrificed for sin. The Hebrew azazel may name the destination ("to the goat that goes away") or a wilderness demon. William Tyndale coined the English word "scape-goat" for this Levitical figure.
scriptures: Leviticus 16:21-22

And Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions in all their sins, putting them upon the head of the goat, and shall send him away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness: And the goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities unto a land not inhabited.
Hebrews 9:28
So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many.
Isaiah 53:6
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
corruption_summary: Modern "scapegoat" means "unfair blame-taker" with negative connotations; the original ritual was substitutionary atonement-symbol.
corruption_paragraphs: Today "scapegoat" implies injustice — an innocent party unfairly blamed. The Levitical ritual was different: a divinely appointed substitute carried sins away by God's command. Christ on the cross is both: rejected by men unjustly (the negative sense) and appointed by God as the sin-bearer (the original ritual sense).
Recover the typology: the two goats together preach the cross. One dies (paying the penalty); one is sent away (removing the stain). Christ does both.
usage: The two goats together preach the cross.
One pays; one removes.
Christ is both.

etymology: Hebrew tzitzit (צִיצִת) — tassel, fringe; commanded in Num 15:38-39 and Deut 22:12.
biblical_def: The tassels Israelites were commanded to wear on the corners of their garments — with a thread of blue — as a visible reminder to keep the commandments of the LORD. The woman with the issue of blood touched the tzitzit of Jesus' garment (Matt 9:20).
webster_summary: Commanded tassels; reminder to keep YHWH's commandments.
webster_full: The tassels (fringes) Israelites were commanded to wear on the corners of their garments, with a single thread of blue, as a visible reminder to keep the LORD's commandments and to refuse following after their own hearts and eyes (Num 15:38-39). Jesus wore them; the woman with the issue of blood touched His tzitzit (Matt 9:20 — "the hem of his garment").
scriptures: Numbers 15:38-39

Speak unto the children of Israel, and bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue: And it shall be unto you for a fringe, that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD.
Matthew 9:20
And, behold, a woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind him, and touched the hem of his garment.
Malachi 4:2
But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings (literally: in his tzitzit).
corruption_summary: Largely forgotten in Christian Bible reading; the visible-reminder theology of tzitzit gets lost, including its connection to Jesus' clothing.
corruption_paragraphs: Most Christians read past the "hem of his garment" without realizing the woman touched a commanded ritual object. The tzitzit was a Mosaic-law mnemonic — visible thread to remind the wearer to obey. The Greek kraspedon in Matt 9:20 is the LXX's word for tzitzit.

Recover the connection: Jesus kept the law, including its visible reminders. The healing power flowed not from the cloth but from the One who wore the cloth. Malachi 4:2's "healing in his wings" may pun on the same word.
usage: Tzitzit are commanded reminders.
Jesus wore them; the bleeding woman touched them.
Malachi may pun: healing in His wings/tzitzit.

etymology: Hebrew tefillin (תְּפִלִּין) — "prayers," the Hebrew name for what Greek-speakers called phylakteria ("safeguards").
biblical_def: The leather boxes containing four key Torah passages (Exod 13:1-10, 13:11-16; Deut 6:4-9, 11:13-21), bound on forehead and arm during morning prayer in obedience to the literal command "bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes" (Deut 6:8).
webster_summary: Leather scripture-boxes worn on forehead and arm during prayer.
webster_full: The leather boxes worn on forehead and arm during morning Jewish prayer, containing four key Torah passages handwritten on parchment. Hebrew tefillin ("prayers"); Greek phylakteria ("safeguards") — the same word KJV translates as "phylacteries." Jesus wore them; He criticized only their being made wide for show (Matt 23:5).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:8
And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes.
Exodus 13:9
And it shall be for a sign unto thee upon thine hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes, that the LORD's law may be in thy mouth.
Matthew 23:5
But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments.
corruption_summary: Often dismissed by Christians as Pharisaic legalism; missed that Jesus wore them and rebuked only their show-display.
corruption_paragraphs: Many Christians read Matthew 23:5 as Jesus rejecting tefillin entirely. The text is more careful: He rebukes the broadening for show. The practice itself was Mosaic; Jesus kept it.
Recover the principle: visible reminders of the word are not legalism — they become legalism when worn for human approval. The mnemonic itself is good; the heart's display-motive is the corruption.
usage: Tefillin obey Deut 6:8 literally.
Jesus wore them; rebuked only the show-display.
Visible mnemonics of the word are good.

etymology: Hebrew tamid (תָּמִיד) — continually, perpetually; the daily morning and evening burnt offering.
biblical_def: The continual daily burnt offering — one lamb in the morning and one in the evening, perpetually, throughout Israel's generations (Exod 29:38-42; Num 28:3-8). The continuity itself was the testimony: God's worship never paused. Daniel 8 names its cessation as a desolation-marker.
webster_summary: The continual morning-and-evening burnt offering.
webster_full: The continual daily burnt offering commanded in Exodus 29 and Numbers 28: one lamb each morning and one each evening, every day throughout Israel's generations. The Hebrew tamid means "continually," and the daily rhythm itself was theological — God's worship in Israel never paused. Daniel 8:11-14 prophesies the desolating cessation of the tamid; its restoration is part of eschatological renewal.
scriptures: Exodus 29:38-39
Now this is that which thou shalt offer upon the altar; two lambs of the first year day by day continually. The one lamb thou shalt offer in the morning; and the other lamb thou shalt offer at even.
Numbers 28:3-4
This is the offering made by fire which ye shall offer unto the LORD; two lambs of the first year without spot day by day, for a continual burnt offering.
Daniel 8:11
Yea, he magnified himself even to the prince of the host, and by him the daily sacrifice (tamid) was taken away.
corruption_summary: Most Christians don't know the tamid existed; with it, the theology of perpetual worship and its cessation as desolation is dimmer.
corruption_paragraphs: The temple's morning-and-evening lamb was Israel's heartbeat. Christians often miss the continuity-symbol entirely. The Hebrew word tamid is the same word that names continuous prayer in modern Hebrew — the unceasing aspect.
Recover the rhythm: morning and evening lamb. Christ is the final tamid — offered once, but His intercession is continual at the right hand of the Father.
usage: Tamid is the continual daily offering.
Christ is the final tamid; His intercession continues.
Pray morning and evening — the rhythm survives.

etymology: Hebrew shemittah (שְׁמִטָּה) — release, remission; from shamat (to release).
biblical_def: The seventh-year sabbath rest commanded for the land (Lev 25:1-7) and for debt (Deut 15:1-11). The land was to lie fallow; debts between Israelites were to be released. Together with the Jubilee year (every 50th), the shemittah encoded mercy into Israel's economic and agricultural life.
webster_summary: The seventh-year sabbath: land rest + debt release.
webster_full: The seventh-year sabbath commanded in Leviticus 25 and Deuteronomy 15. The land rests fallow (Lev 25:4); Israelite debts are released (Deut 15:1-2); Hebrew slaves go free (Exod 21:2). Together with the Jubilee (the 50th year), the shemittah cycle was Israel's economic-spiritual reset, encoding mercy and trust-in-providence into the calendar.
scriptures: Leviticus 25:4
But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land, a sabbath for the LORD: thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard.
Deuteronomy 15:1-2
At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release. And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it.
Exodus 21:2
If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve: and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing.
corruption_summary: Largely ignored; modern economies have no rest-cycle for land or debt-release built in. The principles of fallow-land and debt-release are mostly lost.
corruption_paragraphs: The shemittah was structural mercy — land rested, debts released, slaves freed. Modern economies have no equivalent. The result is land exhaustion, perpetual debt cycles, and economic structures that crush the poor across generations.
Recover the principle: rest is required, debt-mercy is required, freedom is required. The exact form may not transfer, but the principle stands — built-in mercy is biblical economics.
usage: Shemittah encodes mercy into the calendar.
Land rest + debt release + slave freedom.
The principle survives even where the form does not.

etymology: Hebrew ephah (אֵיפָה) — a dry-measure unit, ~22 liters or ~5/8 of a US bushel.
biblical_def: A standard Mosaic-law dry-measure unit (~22 liters / ~20 dry quarts). The just ephah is required (Lev 19:36). Zechariah's vision of the woman in the ephah-basket (Zech 5:5-11) uses the unit symbolically. Modern usage retains "ephah" only in biblical translation.
webster_summary: Standard Mosaic dry measure (~22 liters); just-ephah was required by law.
webster_full: The standard dry-measure unit in Mosaic law, equivalent to about 22 liters (about 20 dry quarts, or 5/8 of a US bushel). Used for grain, flour, and other dry goods. The just ephah was required (Lev 19:36; Deut 25:14-15) — false weights and measures are an abomination. Zechariah 5:5-11 shows a woman (named "Wickedness") sitting in an ephah-basket carried to Babylon, a vision of evil's judgment.
scriptures: Leviticus 19:36
Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt.
Deuteronomy 25:13-15

Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small. Thou shalt not have in thine house divers measures, a great and a small. But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have.
Amos 8:5
Saying, When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel great.
corruption_summary: The just-measures principle has thinned in modern commerce; "shrinkflation" is Amos 8:5 in modern dress.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 8:5 names the merchants who couldn't wait for the sabbath to end so they could cheat with small ephahs and heavy shekels. Modern "shrinkflation" — smaller package, same price — is the exact principle. The LORD hates dishonest measure.
Recover the just measure: in commerce, in promises, in time, in pay. The God who delivered Israel demands honest scales.
usage: Just ephah is required; cheating measures is sin.
Shrinkflation = Amos 8:5 in modern dress.
The God who freed slaves demands honest scales.

etymology: Hebrew omer (עֹמֶר) — a sheaf or a small dry-measure (1/10 of an ephah, ~2 liters).
biblical_def: Two senses: (1) a sheaf of grain — the omer-of-firstfruits waved before YHWH on the day after Passover-Sabbath (Lev 23:10-11); (2) a small dry-measure (one-tenth of an ephah) — the daily portion of manna gathered in the wilderness (Exod 16:16). The 49 days from omer-of-firstfruits to Pentecost are called "counting the omer."
webster_summary: Sheaf of firstfruits; also small dry measure (1/10 ephah).
webster_full: Two distinct senses share the same Hebrew word: (1) a sheaf of grain, especially the omer-of-firstfruits waved before YHWH on the day after the Sabbath of Passover (Lev 23:10-11) — the offering Christ fulfills as "the firstfruits of them that slept" (1 Cor 15:20); (2) a small dry-measure unit equal to one-tenth of an ephah, used for the daily ration of manna in the wilderness (Exod 16:16). The 49 days between the firstfruits omer and Pentecost are still called Sefirat HaOmer (counting the omer).
scriptures: Leviticus 23:10-11

When ye be come into the land which I give unto you, and shall reap the harvest thereof, then ye shall bring a sheaf (omer) of the firstfruits of your harvest unto the priest: And he shall wave the sheaf before the LORD, to be accepted for you.
Exodus 16:16
Gather of it every man according to his eating, an omer for every man.
1 Corinthians 15:20
But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
corruption_summary: The connection between Levitical firstfruits-omer and Christ's resurrection on the same day gets lost in translations that simply say "sheaf."
corruption_paragraphs: Christ rose on the day of the firstfruits-omer wave-offering. Paul calls Him "firstfruits of them that slept" because the timing was deliberate. The Levitical calendar prophesies the gospel calendar.

Recover the omer-pattern: Christ as omer-of-firstfruits, the 49 days of counting the omer leading to Pentecost as Spirit's outpouring (Acts 2). The whole spring feasts cycle preaches the resurrection sequence.
usage: Christ is the firstfruits-omer wave offering.
Counting the omer leads to Pentecost.
Manna by the omer per person, daily.

etymology: Hebrew hin (הִין) — a liquid-measure unit, ~3.7 liters or ~1 gallon.
biblical_def: The standard Mosaic-law liquid-measure unit (~3.7 liters / ~1 US gallon). Used for oil, wine, and water in tabernacle offerings. The just hin is required (Lev 19:36) alongside the just ephah; honest measures are part of righteousness.
webster_summary: Standard Mosaic liquid measure (~3.7 liters / ~1 gallon).
webster_full: The standard liquid-measure unit in Mosaic law, equivalent to about 3.7 liters (about 1 US gallon). Used for oil, wine, and water in tabernacle offerings: a fourth-hin of oil with a tenth-ephah of flour for the meal-offering, etc. The just hin is required (Lev 19:36) alongside the just ephah.
scriptures: Leviticus 19:36
Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God.
Numbers 28:5
And a tenth part of an ephah of flour for a meat offering, mingled with the fourth part of an hin of beaten oil.
Ezekiel 45:24
And he shall prepare a meat offering of an ephah for a ram, and an ephah for a bullock, and an hin of oil for an ephah.
corruption_summary: Lost from common usage; the just-measures principle largely operationalized differently in modern commerce, often badly.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern liquid measures are highly regulated — in theory. In practice, dishonest measures recur: thinned wine, watered milk, deceptive packaging. The hin and ephah laws apply in principle wherever measures are used.
Recover the principle: just measures are part of righteousness. Quietly check that your weights are honest.
usage: Just hin: ~1 gallon liquid measure.
Used with ephah of flour in meal offerings.
Honest measures = righteousness.

etymology: Hebrew shekel ha-qodesh (שֶׁקֶל הַקֹּדֶשׁ) — the temple-standard shekel, distinct from the common-market shekel.
biblical_def: The standardized weight-of-silver used for tabernacle and temple offerings, set apart from the variable common shekel. Half a sanctuary-shekel was the redemption-price for each Israelite male in the census (Exod 30:13-16). The standardization itself was theological — YHWH's worship is not subject to market fluctuation.
webster_summary: The standardized temple-shekel (~11 grams of silver).
webster_full: The standardized shekel weight used for tabernacle and temple offerings, distinct from the common shekel which varied with markets. Approximately 11 grams of silver. Half-a-sanctuary-shekel was the redemption price each Israelite male paid in the census (Exod 30:13). The standardization itself was theological: YHWH's worship is fixed, not subject to inflation or local variation.
scriptures: Exodus 30:13

This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD.
Leviticus 27:25
And all thy estimations shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary.
Matthew 17:24-27
And when they were come to Capernaum, they that received tribute money came to Peter... [Christ pays the half-shekel temple tax through the fish's mouth.]
corruption_summary: Largely lost as a category; modern Christians don't know there were two shekel-standards, much less the theological point.
corruption_paragraphs: The two-shekel system tells us something: God's worship economy is separate from the market. The sanctuary-shekel never varied; the common shekel did. Money used for the LORD must be measured by His standard, not by the market's.
Recover the principle: when you give to God, use His scale. The tithe of grain doesn't shrink because the market-grain shrank.
usage: Sanctuary-shekel is fixed; common-shekel varies.
Half-shekel was the redemption price per male.
God's worship economy is set apart from market.

etymology: Hebrew Har Gerizim (הַר גְּרִזִּים) — "Mount Gerizim," the mountain of blessing in the Joshua covenant ceremony (Deut 11:29; Josh 8:33).
biblical_def: The mountain near Shechem from which the blessings of the covenant were pronounced when Israel entered the land (Deut 27:11-12; Josh 8:33). Counterpart to Mount Ebal, the curse-mountain. Later the Samaritan worship-center; the woman at the well asked Jesus about it (John 4:20).
webster_summary: The mountain of blessing in Joshua's covenant ceremony.
webster_full: The mountain near Shechem from which the blessings of the Sinai covenant were pronounced when Israel entered the land — six tribes stood on Gerizim and answered "amen" to the blessings, while six stood on Mount Ebal opposite and answered "amen" to the curses. Later the Samaritan religious center; the Samaritan woman at the well referenced it (John 4:20). Jesus' answer transcended the mountain dispute: "the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father."
scriptures: Deuteronomy 27:12
These shall stand upon mount Gerizim to bless the people, when ye are come over Jordan; Simeon, and Levi, and Judah, and Issachar, and Joseph, and Benjamin.
Joshua 8:33

And all Israel, and their elders, and officers, and their judges, stood on this side the ark and on that side before the priests the Levites... half of them over against mount Gerizim, and half of them over against mount Ebal.

Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship. Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.
corruption_summary: The blessing-curse covenant ceremony at the entry to the land is largely forgotten; with it, the seriousness of covenant blessing-and-curse fades.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 8 dramatically stages Israel's entry into the land: half the tribes on Gerizim shouting "amen" to blessings, half on Ebal shouting "amen" to curses. The covenant cuts both ways. Modern preaching often takes the blessings without the curses.
Recover the seriousness: the same covenant that promises blessing for obedience promises curse for disobedience. Christ became the curse for us (Gal 3:13) so we might receive the blessing.
usage: Mount of blessing in the Joshua ceremony.
Six tribes shouted amen to blessings.
Christ became the curse so we receive the blessing.

etymology: Hebrew Har Eval (הַר עֵיבָל) — "Mount Ebal," the mountain of curse in the Joshua covenant ceremony.
biblical_def: The mountain near Shechem from which the curses of the covenant were pronounced when Israel entered the land (Deut 27:13; Josh 8:33). Counterpart to Mount Gerizim. Joshua built an altar there of unhewn stones and wrote a copy of the law on plastered stones (Josh 8:30-32).
webster_summary: The mountain of curse in Joshua's covenant ceremony.
webster_full: The mountain near Shechem from which the curses of the Sinai covenant were pronounced when Israel entered the land. Six tribes stood on Ebal and answered "amen" to twelve curses (Deut 27:14-26), while six stood opposite on Mount Gerizim. Joshua built an altar of unhewn stones on Ebal and wrote a copy of the law on plastered stones (Josh 8:30-32) — a 2019 archaeological lead-curse find may corroborate this account.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 27:13
And these shall stand upon mount Ebal to curse; Reuben, Gad, and Asher, and Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali.
Joshua 8:30-32

Then Joshua built an altar unto the LORD God of Israel in mount Ebal, As Moses the servant of the LORD commanded the children of Israel, as it is written in the book of the law of Moses, an altar of whole stones.
Galatians 3:13
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.
corruption_summary: The curse-mountain is forgotten or softened; without Ebal, Christ's becoming-the-curse loses its force.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern preaching loves Gerizim's blessings and avoids Ebal's curses. The covenant ceremony required both. Galatians 3:13 only makes sense against Ebal: Christ "became a curse for us" because the curses of Ebal demanded a bearer.
Recover the dual mountain: the same gospel that gives blessing-of-Gerizim through Christ rescues us from curse-of-Ebal through Him also. Both mountains preach the cross.
usage: Ebal is the curse-mountain.
Christ became the curse-of-Ebal.
Both mountains preach the cross.

etymology: The Hebrew autumn (Tishri) feast cycle: Trumpets, Atonement, Tabernacles — Yamim Noraim (Days of Awe) into Sukkot.
biblical_def: The autumn cluster of feasts in the seventh month (Tishri): Trumpets / Yom Teruah (1st), Day of Atonement / Yom Kippur (10th), and Tabernacles / Sukkot (15th-22nd). Together they mark Israel's high holy season — convocation, repentance, and dwelling. Eschatologically anticipate the consummation cycle (Christ's return, final judgment, eternal dwelling).
webster_summary: Tishri-month autumn feasts: Trumpets, Atonement, Tabernacles.
webster_full: The autumn feast cluster in the seventh month (Tishri): Yom Teruah (Day of Trumpets, 1st of Tishri), Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement, 10th), and Sukkot (Tabernacles, 15th-22nd). Together with the spring feasts and the summer Pentecost, they comprise the Mosaic festal calendar. The fall feasts are typologically eschatological, anticipating Christ's return (trumpet), final atonement consummation, and the eternal dwelling (tabernacles).
scriptures: Leviticus 23:23-44
And the LORD spake unto Moses... in the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation.
Zechariah 14:16

And it shall come to pass, that every one that is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall even go up from year to year to worship the King, the LORD of hosts, and to keep the feast of tabernacles.
1 Thessalonians 4:16
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God.
corruption_summary: Most Christians know little of the autumn feasts; their typological connection to the second coming and final state goes unnoticed.
corruption_paragraphs: Spring feasts (Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Pentecost) preached the first coming and were fulfilled in Christ's death, resurrection, and Spirit-pouring. The fall feasts (Trumpets, Atonement, Tabernacles) preach the second coming and await fulfillment.
Recover the rhythm: the trumpet calls; the atonement-judgment falls; the dwelling is consummated. The Mosaic calendar is the gospel's outline.
usage: Spring feasts: first coming. Fall feasts: second coming.
Trumpet, atonement, dwelling.
The Mosaic calendar is the gospel's outline.

etymology: The Hebrew spring feast cluster: Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, plus Pentecost (Weeks) seven weeks later.
biblical_def: The spring cluster of feasts in Nisan (1st month): Passover (14th), Unleavened Bread (15th-21st), Firstfruits (16th, day after the Sabbath of Passover); plus Pentecost / Weeks 50 days later (in Sivan). All four were fulfilled in Christ's death, resurrection, and Spirit-pouring.
webster_summary: Nisan-month spring feasts + Pentecost: all fulfilled in Christ.
webster_full: The spring feast cluster, all fulfilled in Christ's death, resurrection, and Spirit-pouring: Passover (Christ our Passover sacrificed for us, 1 Cor 5:7); Unleavened Bread (purging of leaven = sin); Firstfruits (Christ the firstfruits of them that slept, 1 Cor 15:20); and Pentecost / Weeks 50 days later (the Spirit poured out, Acts 2). The fulfillment was so precise that the dates aligned exactly.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 5:7
Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.
1 Corinthians 15:20
But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
Acts 2:1
And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place.
corruption_summary: Christians celebrate Easter without realizing the layered fulfillment of three (or four) Levitical feasts in Christ's resurrection week.
corruption_paragraphs: Easter weekend in Christian terms collapses what was a layered Mosaic festal sequence: Passover (Friday's death), Unleavened Bread (Saturday's tomb), Firstfruits (Sunday's resurrection), and Pentecost (50 days later, Spirit). All four feasts fulfilled on their precise dates.
Recover the precision: this wasn't accidental timing. The spring feasts are the gospel's first half of the calendar; the fall feasts await the second half.
usage: Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Pentecost.
All fulfilled exactly on their Mosaic dates.
Spring feasts: first coming.

etymology: Hebrew chattat (חַטָּאת) — both "sin" and "sin-offering"; the Hebrew uses one word for both.
biblical_def: The Mosaic sin-offering (Lev 4) for unintentional sins. Same Hebrew word as "sin" itself — the sin and the offering that addressed it shared a name. Christ was "made sin" (2 Cor 5:21) where the same word-play likely echoes.
webster_summary: The Mosaic sin-offering for unintentional sin (Lev 4).
webster_full: The Mosaic sin-offering described in Leviticus 4. The same Hebrew word means both "sin" and "sin-offering" — the sin and the sacrifice that addressed it shared a name. The blood was applied to the horns of the altar; the rest of the animal was burned outside the camp (a detail Hebrews 13:11-13 develops Christologically). Paul's "made him to be sin for us" (2 Cor 5:21) likely echoes the chattat word-play.
scriptures: Leviticus 4:3

If the priest that is anointed do sin according to the sin of the people; then let him bring for his sin (chattat), which he hath sinned, a young bullock without blemish unto the LORD for a sin offering (chattat).
2 Corinthians 5:21
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
Hebrews 13:11-13

For the bodies of those beasts, whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin, are burned without the camp. Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate.
corruption_summary: The chattat word-play (sin = sin-offering) is invisible in English; with it, the depth of Paul's "made him to be sin" is dimmer.
corruption_paragraphs: English uses two words: sin and sin-offering. Hebrew uses one: chattat. Christ "made sin" in 2 Cor 5:21 likely echoes the chattat language directly — He became the sin-offering, identified so completely with the sin that the same word names them both.
Recover the Levitical-Pauline link: Christ as chattat is the gospel in Hebrew word-economy.
usage: Same Hebrew word: sin / sin-offering.
Christ "made sin" echoes chattat.
Burned outside the camp; Christ outside the gate.

etymology: Hebrew asham (אָשָׁם) — guilt, trespass, guilt-offering. Distinct from chattat (sin / sin-offering).
biblical_def: The Mosaic guilt or trespass offering (Lev 5:14-19; 6:1-7) for sins requiring restitution — usually involving sacred property or harm to neighbor. Required sacrifice plus restitution-plus-fifth-part. Isaiah 53:10 names the Suffering Servant's soul as asham — an offering for guilt.
webster_summary: The Mosaic trespass-offering with restitution-plus-fifth.
webster_full: The Mosaic guilt or trespass offering (Lev 5:14-19; 6:1-7). Distinct from the chattat (sin offering): the asham is for sins involving sacred property or harm to neighbor, requires restitution-plus-a-fifth in addition to sacrifice. Isaiah 53:10 names the Suffering Servant's soul as asham — an offering for guilt — making Christ the ultimate guilt-bearer who pays both God and the wronged.
scriptures: Leviticus 6:5-6

He shall even restore it in the principal, and shall add the fifth part more thereto, and give it unto him to whom it appertaineth, in the day of his trespass offering. And he shall bring his trespass offering unto the LORD.
Isaiah 53:10
Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin (asham), he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days.
Numbers 5:7
Then they shall confess their sin which they have done: and he shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part thereof.
corruption_summary: The restitution-with-sacrifice principle gets dropped; cheap-grace theology accepts forgiveness without the restitution Scripture requires.
corruption_paragraphs: The asham required both sacrifice and restitution-plus-fifth. Forgiveness from God did not erase the obligation to make right with the wronged neighbor. Modern cheap-grace theology often skips the restitution.
Recover the both-and: Christ paid the asham as substitute, and we still owe restitution where possible. Forgiven sin can still owe a fifth part to the wronged.
usage: Asham requires sacrifice + restitution-plus-fifth.
Christ as asham (Isa 53:10) is the gospel.
Forgiven sin can still owe restitution.

etymology: Hebrew zebach (זֶבַח) — sacrifice, especially the peace-offering / fellowship-offering of Lev 3.
biblical_def: The Mosaic peace-offering (Lev 3) — the only Levitical sacrifice in which the worshipper ate the meat as a fellowship-meal with God and others. Distinct from the burnt-offering (entirely consumed). The zebach symbolized covenant fellowship; eating together is the picture of shalom with God.
webster_summary: The Mosaic peace-offering — fellowship-meal with God.
webster_full: The Mosaic peace-offering / fellowship-offering described in Leviticus 3 and 7:11-21. Distinguished from the burnt-offering (entirely consumed on the altar) by the meal-element: the worshipper, the priest, and (representatively) God shared in the meat. The zebach symbolizes covenant shalom — eating together with God. Anticipates the Lord's Supper, the ultimate fellowship-meal.
scriptures: Leviticus 3:1
And if his oblation be a sacrifice (zebach) of peace offering, if he offer it of the herd; whether it be a male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the LORD.
Leviticus 7:15
And the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten the same day that it is offered.
Luke 22:20
This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.
corruption_summary: Christians often skip Leviticus, missing how the peace-offering's meal-fellowship anticipates the Lord's Supper.
corruption_paragraphs: Sacrifice in modern religious vocabulary suggests destruction (the burnt-offering). The zebach is different — a meal shared. The blood addresses sin; the eaten meat celebrates restored fellowship. The Lord's Supper inherits this shape.
Recover the meal: communion is not just memorial — it is the new-covenant zebach, the meal of restored shalom with the Father through the Son.
usage: Zebach is the meal-sacrifice.
Lord's Supper inherits the zebach-shape.
Eating together: the picture of shalom.

etymology: Hebrew olah (עֹלָה) — literally "that which goes up"; the burnt-offering entirely consumed on the altar.
biblical_def: The Mosaic burnt-offering (Lev 1) — the sacrifice entirely consumed by fire on the altar, ascending as smoke to YHWH. The most fundamental Levitical sacrifice. Symbolized total dedication. The continual tamid burnt-offering ran morning and evening forever in Israel's temple.
webster_summary: The Mosaic burnt-offering — entirely consumed; total dedication.
webster_full: The Mosaic burnt-offering described in Leviticus 1. The sacrifice entirely consumed by fire on the altar, ascending as smoke to YHWH (hence the name olah, "that which goes up"). The most fundamental and frequent Levitical sacrifice. Symbolized total dedication; the worshipper kept nothing back. Christ as olah (Eph 5:2) gave Himself wholly.
scriptures: Leviticus 1:9
But his inwards and his legs shall he wash in water: and the priest shall burn all on the altar, to be a burnt sacrifice (olah), an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD.
Genesis 22:2
And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering.
Ephesians 5:2
And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour.
corruption_summary: Sacrifice-language in modern usage carries either negative connotation (giving something up bitterly) or self-congratulatory connotation ("I sacrificed for them"); the total-dedication-to-God shape of olah gets dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "sacrifice" sounds either bitter or self-congratulatory. Hebrew olah is total dedication — everything ascending, nothing kept. The worshipper gives the whole animal; God receives the whole. Christ is the perfect olah: He gave Himself wholly.
Recover the total-ness: living-sacrifice in Romans 12:1 is olah-language. Present your bodies, the whole.
usage: Olah is total ascending dedication.
Christ is the perfect olah.
Living-sacrifice is olah-language.

etymology: Hebrew minchah (מִנְחָה) — tribute, gift, grain-offering. KJV often translates "meat offering" using older English where "meat" meant any food.
biblical_def: The Mosaic grain-offering (Lev 2) — fine flour with oil and frankincense, sometimes baked, sometimes raw, never with leaven or honey. Accompanied animal sacrifices and was sometimes offered alone. Represented the consecration of the worshipper's labor (bread, the work of human hands).
webster_summary: The Mosaic grain-offering — consecrated labor's fruit.
webster_full: The Mosaic grain-offering described in Leviticus 2. Fine flour with oil and frankincense, sometimes baked, sometimes raw, never with leaven or honey, always with salt. Accompanied animal sacrifices; could also be offered alone. Represented the consecration of the worshipper's labor (bread is the work of human hands). KJV translates with the older English "meat offering" (where "meat" simply meant food).
scriptures: Leviticus 2:1
And when any will offer a meat offering (minchah) unto the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon.
Leviticus 2:13
And every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering.
Malachi 1:11
For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering.
corruption_summary: KJV's "meat offering" confuses modern readers (it's grain, not meat); the consecration-of-labor theology gets thinned in modern Bible reading.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern English "meat" means animal flesh; older English "meat" meant any food. KJV's "meat offering" is the minchah, a grain-offering — bread for God. The consecration represented the worshipper's labor (someone planted, harvested, ground, mixed, baked).

Recover the consecration of labor: when Paul says "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord" (Col 3:23), he is in minchah-territory. Every loaf of bread your work produces can be offered, in spirit, to the LORD.
usage: Minchah is grain (not "meat" in modern sense).
Bread = consecrated labor.
Work as worship; offering as life.

etymology: The lunisolar calendar prescribed in Mosaic law and still used in Jewish religious life. Months are lunar; intercalation by an extra Adar keeps Passover in spring.
biblical_def: The lunisolar calendar of the Mosaic law (still used liturgically by Jews and key to understanding Bible chronology). Twelve lunar months, with a thirteenth (Adar II) added in seven of every nineteen years to keep the calendar synchronized with the solar year. The religious year begins in Nisan; the civil year in Tishri.
webster_summary: The lunisolar Mosaic calendar; basis of the feasts.
webster_full: The lunisolar calendar prescribed in Mosaic law: twelve lunar months (Nisan, Iyar, Sivan, Tammuz, Av, Elul, Tishri, Cheshvan, Kislev, Tevet, Shevat, Adar) with a thirteenth (Adar II) intercalated seven times in every nineteen-year cycle to keep the calendar in sync with the solar year. The religious year starts in Nisan (spring); the civil year in Tishri (autumn). The calendar's structure encodes the feast cycle — spring, summer, fall — that frames Israel's worship-year.
scriptures: Exodus 12:2
This month (Nisan) shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you.
Leviticus 23:1-44
[The whole chapter detailing the feasts of the LORD according to their seasons.]
Galatians 4:4
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law.
corruption_summary: Christian use of Gregorian calendar disconnects readers from the Hebraic calendar's structure, which the Bible's own chronology assumes.
corruption_paragraphs: The Bible's calendar is Hebraic. Passover is in Nisan; Pentecost is fifty days after Passover Sabbath; Yom Kippur is on the tenth of Tishri; Sukkot starts on the fifteenth. Reading these references through Gregorian lenses ("April" or "October") obscures the structure.
Recover the calendar: the spring-summer-fall feast cycle is the Bible's own rhythm. The fullness of the time (Gal 4:4) was Hebraic-calendar specific.
roots_summary: Hebrew calendar months and feast cycle.
usage: Twelve lunar months + intercalary Adar II.
Religious year starts Nisan; civil year Tishri.
Bible chronology assumes Hebraic dating.

etymology: Hebrew chag (חַג) — pilgrimage feast; from a root meaning "to dance, to make a circuit." Cognate to Arabic hajj.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for the three pilgrimage feasts — Passover, Pentecost (Weeks), and Tabernacles — at which all male Israelites were required to appear before YHWH at Jerusalem (Exod 23:14-17; Deut 16:16). Distinguished from other holy days; chag specifically means a pilgrimage festival.
webster_summary: Hebrew "feast" — specifically the three pilgrimage festivals.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for the three annual pilgrimage feasts at which all male Israelites were required to appear at the central sanctuary: Passover (with Unleavened Bread), Weeks / Pentecost, and Tabernacles. Distinct from other holy days. The same root underlies Arabic hajj. Christ as a Jewish male went up to Jerusalem for the chagim regularly (e.g., John 7's Sukkot).
scriptures: Exodus 23:14
Three times thou shalt keep a feast (chag) unto me in the year.
Deuteronomy 16:16

Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the LORD thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles.
John 7:14
Now about the midst of the feast (chag, here Sukkot) Jesus went up into the temple, and taught.
corruption_summary: Most Christians use "feast" for any biblical festival; the specific chag (pilgrimage) category gets blurred.
corruption_paragraphs: Three feasts are chagim (pilgrimage); others are not. The distinction matters: the chagim demanded physical pilgrimage to the central sanctuary, costly and disruptive of normal life. Israel's rhythms were set by these required journeys.
Recover the pilgrimage shape: faith in Scripture is repeatedly framed as pilgrimage to a central God-meeting. Hebrews 11 names the patriarchs as pilgrims; the saint walks the same road.
usage: Three chagim: Passover, Weeks, Tabernacles.
Pilgrimage to the central sanctuary.
Faith is pilgrimage-shaped.

etymology: From the Mosaic law's central principle: "the life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul" (Lev 17:11).
biblical_def: The blood of sacrificial animals (and supremely of Christ) by which atonement was made for sin. Leviticus 17:11 is the foundational principle: life is in blood; blood makes atonement; atonement is by life-given-for-life. Hebrews 9:22: "without shedding of blood is no remission."
webster_summary: Sacrificial blood by which atonement is made; principle of life-for-life.
webster_full: The blood of sacrificial animals (and supremely of Christ) by which atonement was made. Leviticus 17:11 names the principle: "the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul." Atonement is by life-substituted-for-life. Hebrews 9:22 makes the principle universal: "without shedding of blood is no remission."
scriptures: Leviticus 17:11
For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.
Hebrews 9:22
And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.
1 John 1:7
And the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.
corruption_summary: Modern squeamishness about blood and substitution makes this central biblical theology hard to hear; "blood theology" gets dismissed as primitive.
corruption_paragraphs: The age finds blood-talk disturbing. Scripture is unflinching: life is in blood; sin requires life; atonement is by life-given. Christ's blood is not metaphor or symbol; it is the actual life of the perfect Substitute given for the saved.

Recover the blood theology without flinching: "there is a fountain filled with blood, drawn from Immanuel's veins" is not Victorian sentiment — it is Hebrew theology. The blood cleanses because the blood was life poured out.
usage: Life is in blood; atonement requires life.
Without shedding of blood is no remission.
Christ's blood cleanses from all sin.

etymology: The eight specific garments of the Aaronic high priest detailed in Exodus 28: ephod, breastplate, robe, tunic, miter, sash, breeches, and the gold plate ("Holiness to the LORD").
biblical_def: The eight garments commanded for the Aaronic high priest in Exodus 28: ephod (gold-blue-purple-scarlet vestment), breastplate of judgment (with twelve gemstones for the tribes and the Urim and Thummim), robe of the ephod (with bells and pomegranates), broidered tunic, miter / turban, embroidered sash, linen breeches, and the gold plate inscribed "Holiness to the LORD" (Qodesh la-YHWH) on the forehead. Together they were "for glory and for beauty" (Exod 28:2).
webster_summary: The eight Aaronic high-priest garments of Exodus 28.
webster_full: The eight specific garments commanded for the Aaronic high priest, detailed in Exodus 28-29: ephod, breastplate of judgment with twelve gemstones (one per tribe) and the Urim and Thummim, robe of the ephod (with golden bells and pomegranates around the hem), broidered tunic, miter / turban, embroidered sash, linen breeches, and the gold plate engraved "Holiness to the LORD" worn on the forehead. Together "for glory and for beauty." The high priest carried Israel's tribes on his shoulders and over his heart.
scriptures: Exodus 28:2
And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother for glory and for beauty.
Exodus 28:29-30

And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart, when he goeth in unto the holy place, for a memorial before the LORD continually. And thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim.
Hebrews 9:11-12
But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands... by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place.
corruption_summary: Most Christians read past Exodus 28; the typological richness of the high priest's garments and their fulfillment in Christ goes unnoticed.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 28 is one of the most lavishly detailed chapters in Scripture for a reason: the garments preach. Christ as High Priest carries His people on His shoulders (strength) and over His heart (love); His holiness is visible (forehead plate); the bells of His robe sound in the holy place (continual intercession heard).
Recover the typology: every detail of the garments preaches the high priestly ministry of Christ. Hebrews 7-10 unpacks it; the saint should read Exodus 28 with that lens.
roots_summary: Hebrew terms for each garment in Exodus 28.
usage: For glory and for beauty.
Tribes on shoulders and over heart.
Christ as the fulfilling High Priest.

etymology: Hebrew goel ha-dam (גֹּאֵל הַדָּם) — "the redeemer of blood," the kinsman with right and obligation to avenge the blood of a slain relative (Num 35:19; Deut 19:6).
biblical_def: The Mosaic-law office of the kinsman responsible for executing justice on the slayer of a blood-relative — literally "redeemer of blood." Same Hebrew word (goel) as the kinsman-redeemer of Ruth (who redeems land and marries the widow). One word, three offices: avenger of blood, redeemer of land, marrier of widows. All three converge in Christ.
webster_summary: The Mosaic kinsman-avenger; same word as kinsman-redeemer.
webster_full: The Mosaic-law office of the kinsman charged with executing justice on the slayer of a blood-relative. Hebrew goel ha-dam uses the same root goel as the kinsman-redeemer of Ruth (who redeems family land and marries the childless widow). One word, three offices: avenger of blood, redeemer of property, marrier of widow. The Mosaic cities of refuge bounded the goel-ha-dam's pursuit; the high priest's death released the manslayer. All three offices converge in Christ — our Goel.
scriptures: Numbers 35:19
The revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer: when he meeteth him, he shall slay him.
Ruth 4:14
Blessed be the LORD, which hath not left thee this day without a kinsman, that his name may be famous in Israel.
For I know that my redeemer (goel) liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth.
corruption_summary: The unity of the three goel-offices is invisible in English (different words used for each); the Christ-as-Goel theology dims with it.
corruption_paragraphs: English splits the goel into three roles (avenger of blood, kinsman-redeemer, levir); Hebrew uses one word. Christ unifies the offices: He avenges (sin's blood is paid), He redeems (the lost inheritance is bought back), He marries (the widow-bride is taken).
Recover the unity: when Job cries "I know that my Redeemer liveth" (goali chai), he is invoking the comprehensive office. Christ is our Goel in every direction.
usage: One Hebrew word: avenger, redeemer, marrier.
Christ is our Goel in every direction.
Job's goali chai = my Redeemer liveth.
